t: Number of Times Binary String Is Prefix-Aligned — Editorial
o: We flip one bit per step, and after each step we ask: are exactly the first i bits (where i is the step number) set to 1? Since flips is a permutation of [1, n], after step i exactly i bits are 1. The string is prefix-aligned at step i if and only if the set of flipped positions so far is exactly {1, 2, ..., i}. In Example 1, the first three steps flip 3, 2, 4 — the max seen is 4 but only 3 bits are on, so it fails; at step 4 we've flipped {1,2,3,4} with max 4, which matches. Constraints allow n up to 5·10^4, so an O(n) or O(n log n) single pass is more than sufficient; no simulation of strings is needed.
k: After step i, exactly i bits are 1, so prefix-aligned means the maximum flipped position equals i.
Track a running maximum while scanning flips; count steps where max == current index.
No string simulation is needed — the permutation property makes the check O(1) per step.

a.i: After step i, the number of 1-bits is exactly i. The bits in positions [1, i] are all 1 iff every flipped position so far is ≤ i, and since there are i of them (all distinct), that's equivalent to the maximum flipped position being exactly i. So we just scan once, maintain the running max, and increment the answer whenever max == i. This works because flips is a permutation — no duplicates or gaps to worry about.
s: For each index i from 0 to n-1, update mx = max(mx, flips[i]).
If mx == i + 1, increment ans (the string is prefix-aligned at this step).
a.t: O(n) — a single pass over flips with constant work per element.
a.sp: O(1) — only two scalar variables beyond the input.

a.i: A neat variant: after step i, the sum of flipped values equals the sum 1+2+...+i = i(i+1)/2 iff the flipped set is exactly {1,...,i} (all values distinct and positive). So compare the running sum of flips[0..i] against the triangular number i(i+1)/2. This avoids tracking a max and generalizes nicely as a trick, though it's equally O(n).
s: For each index i from 0 to n-1, add flips[i] to s.
The expected triangular number is (i+1)(i+2)/2; if s equals it, increment ans.
a.t: O(n) — one pass with constant work per step.
a.sp: O(1) — only running sum and counter; use 64-bit sums since total can reach ~1.25·10^9.

w: In an interview, lead with the running-maximum approach: it's the simplest and most direct application of the key insight that 'exactly i ones' plus 'max position = i' forces the prefix to be fully lit. The sum approach is a nice alternative worth mentioning. Common pitfalls: off-by-one errors between 0-indexed loops and 1-indexed bit positions (compare mx with i+1); assuming you need to simulate the string (unnecessary and wasteful); in C++/Java, watch overflow if using the sum method without 64-bit integers. Edge cases: n = 1 always returns 1; the last step is always prefix-aligned, so the answer is at least 1. Follow-ups might include handling non-permutation inputs (then you'd need a count of zeros in the prefix, e.g., via a BIT or counting flipped positions), or streaming versions where flips arrives online.
